reason: REFUTED on minted punctuation. The evidence claims two independent texts were compared line by line, and both of them contradict the shipped wording at exactly the point the evidence does not mention. PG ebook 8604 (the named House of Atreus) prints the Watchman sixth line as The starry conclave of the midnight sky, with a COMMA, and the Wikisource Morshead text prints the same comma. The sentence does not stop there: it runs on for four more lines and ends at The year’s divisions, bringing frost or fire. The shipped line silently turns that comma into a full stop so as to satisfy the rule that a quotation ends in a full stop. That is minting the edition punctuation, which rule 12 forbids, and it is precisely the thing the same verifier DID disclose for 10-poet-02 and did not disclose here, so the evidence overstates what was checked. Everything else about the entry holds, which is why the fix is a re-cut and not a deletion: the five preceding lines match both texts exactly, the 1881 first edition and the 1889 second edition are real (C. Kegan Paul, 1881; Morshead 1849 to 1912), shipped.js returns not shipped, no near match, aeschylus 1 of 3 standing in month 7 only, not banned, the tag Drama is the form, and the source line is 102 characters with the speaker after the locator. THE FIX: cut at line 10, the first genuine full stop, and ship I pray the gods to quit me of my toils, / To close the watch I keep, this livelong year; / For as a watch-dog lying, not at rest, / Propped on one arm, upon the palace-roof / Of Atreus’ race, too long, too well I know / The starry conclave of the midnight sky, / Too well, the splendours of the firmament, / The lords of light, whose kingly aspect shows— / What time they set or climb the sky in turn— / The year’s divisions, bringing frost or fire. (em dashes inside a quotation are allowed; rule 5 bans them only in the source and the note). SECOND, SOFTER OBJECTION for the editor: even re-cut, the passage is a man begging the gods to release him from a year of sleepless watching, propped on one arm and not at rest. It is a vigil, so it touches the month, but it reads as weariness rather than stillness, and rule 3 asks whether it helps at six in the morning.
